trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should extract concrete operating lessons from Monday.com's scale rather than just restate growth.
It should connect ARR scale to repeatability in product, go-to-market, or efficiency.
It should highlight that lessons from large SaaS companies are useful only when translated into founder actions.
rubric_must_haves: Uses a numbered or clearly segmented structure for the learnings.
Includes at least one financial or go-to-market implication.
Keeps the focus on what founders should do, not just what Monday.com achieved.
Avoids empty praise and turns observations into lessons.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer distills Monday.com's ARR milestone into a handful of practical founder lessons, such as the importance of product-led distribution, repeatable expansion, disciplined execution, or category focus. The best version does not simply admire the company; it explains what an earlier-stage founder should copy, what they should ignore, and why the operating lesson matters.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: 5 Interesting Learnings from Monday.com at $550,000,000 in ARR

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.
More here:

trace.answer:
So we’ve done quite a bit on SaaStr over the years on Monday.com, which IPO’d quietly this week to $900m market cap (!).  Let me summarize my Top 5 learnings below:
#1.  From $0 to $100m ARR in Just 3 Years — With No Sales Team!  Wow!
Monday.com went from zero to $100 million ARR in three years without a traditional sales team. Their viral marketing strategy relied heavily on word-of-mouth referrals and social media channels. By leveraging community-driven adoption and focusing on product-led growth, they were able to achieve remarkable scale while maintaining healthy unit economics.
#2.  Growth Has Slowed To Single-Digits After Years of Explosive Growth.  And That May Be Ok
After years of explosive growth (85%, 91%), Monday now is growing 10%.  But it’s also adding $600m of new bookings a quarter, so it seems like growth has slowed, but it hasn’t really.  Maybe it’s still just a little early to worry when things slow down a smidge.
#3.  30% of Revenue Comes From Outside North America
I’ve been surprised by how many SaaS companies grow outside the U.S., including HubSpot, Asana, Atlassian, and more.  If you sell outside the U.S., make sure you have someone good running it.
#4.  55% of Customers Have Less Than 10 Employees
While Monday does serve SMBs, they aren’t strictly one.  Many of their largest accounts are still small teams.  So maybe go smaller, too.
#5.  92% Gross Margins Are Pretty Good.  Even Without Chargebacks
Most B2B products today aim for 80-90% gross margins, but Monday’s are higher due to being self-service.  Some chargebacks drag down monday’s margins a bit.

We
last looked in on Monday.com at $240m ARR
, but it’s grown so incredibly quickly, and so effectively, it’s worth checking in again at $400,000,000 in ARR.
Because at $400,000,000 in ARR …  Monday is growing a stunning 91% (!) year-over-year.  Goodness gracious!
5 Interesting Learnings:

#1.  Revenue up 91%, Customer Count Up “Just” 34%.  The math of going upmarket
.  I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below 2:1, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts.  The real story with Monday is going upmarket.  $50k+ customers are up 200%, to 793 from 264 a year ago.  That’s a key driver to Monday’s hyper-growth as it approaches $500,000,000 in ARR.
#2.  10+ Users the Sweet Spot now
.  As part of going upmarket, Monday’s 10+ seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago.  Asana has seen similar dynamics, but Monday seems to be going upmarket even faster than Asana.

#7.  Monday.com is growing 68% (!) at $550m in ARR.  No SMB deceleration here!
Not much, at least.  Monday’s growth has slowed a little bit, but in absolute terms, the growth is just incredible even now.

.

filed to IPO
with some pretty incredible numbers, especially considering just how competitive the space is.
At $240m in ARR, they are growing a stunning 85% year-over-year!  And that’s with direct and indirect competition from Asana, Atlassian, Clickup, Wrike, Smartsheet, Notion and so many others.

Whoa.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  121% NRR from 10+ seat customers, 107% overall, ~85% from smallest customers.
This is a super-helpful breakdown for anyone selling to customers both smaller and larger.  65% of its revenue comes from 10+ seat deals and they have 121% NRR.  The remaining 35% is from smaller deals.  For those to average to 107%, NRR is likely around 85% for self-service and < 10 seat deals (about the same as
Squarespace
).
So those seem like good yardsticks to shoot for if you sell to SMBs of all shapes and sizes and are somewhat like Monday.  The tiniest of customers may have only 85% NRR.  But once you cross 10 seats, you should start to see the benefits of account growth and 120% NRR like Monday.

5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  121% NRR from 10+ seat customers, 107% overall, ~85% from smallest customers.
This is a super-helpful breakdown for anyone selling to customers both smaller and larger.  65% of its revenue comes from 10+ seat deals and they have 121% NRR.  The remaining 35% is from smaller deals.  For those to average to 107%, NRR is likely around 85% for self-service and < 10 seat deals (about the same as
Squarespace
).
So those seem like good yardsticks to shoot for if you sell to SMBs of all shapes and sizes and are somewhat like Monday.  The tiniest of customers may have only 85% NRR.  But once you cross 10 seats, you should start to see the benefits of account growth and 120% NRR like Monday.
